lead: This unit covers two families of problems: members in axial compression, and shells under internal pressure. You will see why a long column bends sideways and collapses at a load far below its crushing strength, and how the wall of a cylinder or sphere carries the pressure inside it. After it you can find a safe load for a strut with any end condition, and the stresses and volume change in thin and thick shells.
about: Unit 7 has two halves. Chapters 7.1 to 7.4 treat members in axial compression: how a column differs from a strut, the end conditions that fix the buckled shape, Euler's crippling load, effective length and slenderness ratio, and Rankine-Gordon for columns too short for Euler. Chapters 7.5 to 7.8 turn to pressure vessels: hoop and longitudinal stress in a thin cylinder, the thin sphere and its volume change, then Lame's thick-cylinder stresses when the wall is no longer thin, and finally compound cylinders made by shrink fitting. Each chapter feeds the next: Euler's load becomes a slenderness formula, Rankine patches its short-column failure, and Lame's equations are superposed for compound tubes.

chapters.idea: A member in axial compression fails by bending sideways, and the load it carries depends on how its ends are held, so compression members are classified by behaviour and by end condition.
chapters.depth: Define the axial compression member. A strut is any compression member, at any angle, as in a truss; a column is a vertical compression member, as in a building or a press. Some syllabi use the two words interchangeably. Classification by behaviour: short column fails by crushing, long column fails by buckling at a load well below crushing, intermediate column by a mixture. Describe the five end conditions physically: both ends pinned (hinged), both ends fixed, one fixed and one free (a flagpole), one fixed and one pinned, both ends fixed but free to move sideways. Define area A, least second moment of area I, and radius of gyration r = sqrt(I/A); say clearly that buckling takes the path of least resistance, so I minimum governs. Note that Euler's crippling load, critical load and buckling load mean the same thing.

figure.aria: Tree that sorts compression members into struts and columns, with columns split into short, intermediate and long by how they fail.

chapters.example: A steel rod of diameter d = 30 mm and length 2 m is used (a) as a tie rod in a roof truss and (b) as a vertical strut carrying a compressive load. Find its area, least second moment of area and least radius of gyration, and say which use needs a buckling check. A = pi d^2/4 = 3.1416 x (0.030)^2/4 = 7.069 x 10^-4 m^2. I = pi d^4/64 = 3.1416 x (0.030)^4/64 = 3.976 x 10^-8 m^4. r = sqrt(I/A) = sqrt(3.976 x 10^-8 / 7.069 x 10^-4) = 7.5 x 10^-3 m = 7.5 mm, which is also d/4. The tie carries tension and cannot buckle. The strut is in compression and must be checked for buckling, about any axis, so r does not depend on direction for a solid round rod.
chapters.trap: Using the second moment of area about the strong axis. A column bends about the axis that gives the smallest I, so always take I minimum and r minimum.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for stress, strain and factor of safety; Unit 4 for centroid and second moment of area.
chapters.leave: The derivation of Euler's formula to 7.2; the numerical values of effective length and slenderness ratio to 7.3.

chapters.idea: A perfectly straight pin-ended column buckles at P = pi^2 EI/L^2, and every other end condition uses the same expression with L replaced by an effective length.
chapters.depth: Set up the bent shape: with a small sideways deflection y at distance x, the bending moment is P y, and the bending equation EI d2y/dx2 = -P y gives a sine solution that first becomes possible at the critical load. Carry the derivation for both ends pinned in full. Then state the four standard results as P = pi^2 EI/(K L)^2 with K = 1 (pinned-pinned), 0.5 (fixed-fixed), about 0.7 (fixed-pinned) and 2 (fixed-free). Define E (Young's modulus), I (least second moment of area), L (actual length) and P (crippling load). Show that the buckled shapes differ: one full sine wave, a half wave, and so on. Mention that these are ideal, frictionless ends and real joints sit somewhere between pinned and fixed.

figure.aria: Critical load against length for the four end conditions; the fixed-fixed curve is highest and the fixed-free curve lowest at every length.

chapters.example: A hollow steel tube of outside diameter D = 60 mm, inside diameter d = 50 mm and length L = 3 m is used as a column with E = 200 GPa. Find the crippling load when both ends are pinned, and when both ends are fixed. I = pi (D^4 - d^4)/64 = 3.1416 x (12,960,000 - 6,250,000)/64 = 3.294 x 10^5 mm^4 = 3.294 x 10^-7 m^4. EI = 200 x 10^9 x 3.294 x 10^-7 = 65,880 N m^2. Pinned-pinned: P = pi^2 EI/L^2 = 9.8696 x 65,880 / 3^2 = 72,245 N, about 72.2 kN. Fixed-fixed: the effective length is L/2, so P is four times larger, 288,980 N, about 289 kN. Fixing the ends quadruples the load the same tube can carry.
chapters.trap: Two slips: forgetting I minimum, and squaring L in millimetres while E is in N/m^2. Keep every length in the same unit throughout.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for end conditions and radius of gyration; Unit 4 for the bending equation; Unit 5 for the elastic curve of a bent beam.
chapters.leave: Effective length ratios in a table and the slenderness limits of Euler to 7.3; eccentric loading and the secant formula are outside these chapters.

chapters.idea: Slenderness ratio Le/r decides everything: Euler's critical stress is pi^2 E divided by the square of that ratio, and the formula holds only while this stress stays below the proportional limit.
chapters.depth: Define effective length Le = K L, with K from 7.2, and slenderness ratio lambda = Le/r (no units). Give the standard view that a member is thin or slender when lambda is large, stocky when small; only a few syllabi fix the exact boundary. Derive the critical stress sigma_cr = P/A = pi^2 E/lambda^2. Show that Euler says nothing useful for small lambda, because sigma_cr then climbs above the yield stress, which cannot happen. Find the limit lambda = sqrt(pi^2 E/sigma_c), roughly 89 for mild steel with E = 200 GPa and yield 250 MPa. List the other limits: the formula assumes a perfectly straight, homogeneous, initially stress-free member loaded exactly axially, and it ignores the fact that real ends are neither fully pinned nor fully fixed.

figure.aria: Euler critical stress falling steeply with slenderness; the curve crosses the yield stress line at a slenderness of about 89, and to the left of that point Euler is invalid.

chapters.example: A column has effective length Le = 4.5 m, E = 200 GPa and yield stress 250 MPa. (a) Its least radius of gyration is r = 25 mm. Find lambda and the Euler stress, and say whether Euler applies. (b) Repeat if r = 60 mm. (a) lambda = 4500/25 = 180, sigma_cr = pi^2 E/lambda^2 = 9.8696 x 200,000/180^2 = 60.9 MPa, well below 250 MPa, so Euler applies. (b) lambda = 4500/60 = 75, sigma_cr = 9.8696 x 200,000/75^2 = 350.9 MPa, above the yield stress, so Euler is invalid and the column must be treated as an intermediate column.
chapters.trap: Using the actual length instead of the effective length in lambda, and quoting a Euler load from a stocky column whose computed stress exceeds the yield stress.
chapters.prereq: 7.1 for I minimum and r; 7.2 for Euler's load and the end-condition factors.
chapters.leave: Rankine-Gordon, which covers the short and intermediate range, to 7.4.

chapters.idea: Rankine-Gordon joins crushing and buckling in one formula, P = sigma_c A/(1 + a lambda^2), which is safe at every slenderness.
chapters.depth: Introduce the empirical formula with sigma_c the crushing (compressive yield) stress, A the area, lambda = Le/r and a a material constant. Show the two limits: at small lambda the 1 in the denominator dominates and P tends to sigma_c A; at large lambda the a lambda^2 term dominates and P tends to (sigma_c/a)/lambda^2, which behaves like Euler. Give typical data-book values: cast iron sigma_c = 550 MPa with a = 1/1600; mild steel sigma_c = 320 MPa with a = 1/7500; timber sigma_c = 50 MPa with a = 1/750. Note that a is fitted to test data, close to but not exactly sigma_c/(pi^2 E). Explain why a factor of safety is applied to P, and that the same formula is called Rankine's formula in some books.

figure.title: Which column formula
figure.aria: Flowchart: find the slenderness ratio, test whether the Euler stress stays below yield, then use Rankine-Gordon or Euler accordingly.

chapters.example: A hollow cast iron column of outside diameter D = 200 mm, inside diameter d = 150 mm and length L = 4 m has both ends fixed. Take sigma_c = 550 MPa, a = 1/1600, E = 100 GPa. Find the Rankine load. A = pi (0.2^2 - 0.15^2)/4 = 0.013744 m^2. I = pi (0.2^4 - 0.15^4)/64 = 5.369 x 10^-5 m^4, so r = sqrt(I/A) = 0.0625 m. With both ends fixed Le = 0.5 x 4 = 2 m, so lambda = 2/0.0625 = 32 and lambda^2 = 1024. Then a lambda^2 = 1024/1600 = 0.64, and P = 550 x 10^6 x 0.013744/(1 + 0.64) = 4.61 x 10^6 N, about 4610 kN. Euler with the same data would give about 13,250 kN, four times too high for such a stocky column.
chapters.trap: Feeding L/r instead of Le/r into lambda, and mixing the constant a with a stress. Since a lambda^2 is added to 1, both a and lambda must be used consistently and a must be taken from the data sheet, not invented.
chapters.prereq: 7.2 for Euler's load; 7.3 for slenderness ratio and the Euler limit; Unit 1 for crushing stress and factor of safety.
chapters.leave: Eccentric loading, the secant formula and Perry's formula lie outside these chapters; some syllabi add them after Rankine.

chapters.idea: A thin cylinder under internal pressure carries a hoop stress twice its longitudinal stress, and both follow from a simple force balance on a cut piece of the shell.
chapters.depth: State the thin-wall assumption: wall thickness t is at most one-twentieth of the internal diameter d, so the stress is taken as uniform through the thickness; some books say d/t of 20 or more. Derive the hoop stress by cutting the cylinder along a diameter and balancing the pressure force p d L against 2 sigma_h t L, with p the internal pressure, d the internal diameter, L the length of the cut, t the thickness: sigma_h = p d/(2t). Derive the longitudinal stress by cutting across the axis: sigma_L = p d/(4t) = sigma_h/2. Give the closed-end assumption for sigma_L. Add strains through Hooke's law: epsilon_h = (sigma_h - nu sigma_L)/E, epsilon_L = (sigma_L - nu sigma_h)/E, with E Young's modulus and nu Poisson's ratio, then change in diameter and length. Mention maximum shear stress sigma_h/2 through the wall and (sigma_h - sigma_L)/2 in the surface, briefly, and joint efficiency for a riveted or welded shell.

figure.title: Hoop stress from force balance
figure.aria: Flowchart of the hoop stress derivation, from internal pressure to cutting the shell in half, balancing forces, and reading off hoop and longitudinal stress.

nodes.label: Balance forces
nodes.note: 2 sigma_h t L = p d L

chapters.example: A cylindrical boiler shell of internal diameter d = 1.2 m and thickness t = 8 mm carries steam at p = 1.2 MPa. Take E = 200 GPa and nu = 0.3. Check thinness: d/t = 1200/8 = 150, well above 20. Hoop stress sigma_h = p d/(2t) = 1.2 x 10^6 x 1.2/(2 x 0.008) = 90 MPa. Longitudinal stress sigma_L = p d/(4t) = 45 MPa. Hoop strain epsilon_h = (90 - 0.3 x 45)/200,000 = 76.5/200,000 = 3.825 x 10^-4, so the diameter grows by 1200 x 3.825 x 10^-4 = 0.459 mm.
chapters.trap: Putting the diameter where the radius belongs (the result is the same either way, so the slip hides), and forgetting that the longitudinal stress is half the hoop stress, not equal to it.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for Hooke's law, Poisson's ratio and volumetric strain; Unit 2 for plane stress and Mohr's circle.
chapters.leave: Full volume change of a cylinder and the sphere to 7.6; walls too thick for this assumption to 7.7.

chapters.idea: A thin sphere carries the same stress in every direction, sigma = p d/(4t), so it is twice as strong as a cylinder of the same size, and its volume change follows from three equal strains.
chapters.depth: Derive sigma = p d/(4t) by cutting the sphere through its centre: pressure force p x pi d^2/4 balanced by the stress around the cut circumference pi d t. Show that any cut gives the same result, so there is no direction of weakness and no shear stress on those planes. Strain epsilon = (sigma/E)(1 - nu), because all three direct stresses are equal. Volume strain for the sphere: dV/V = 3 epsilon. For a thin cylinder, derive dV/V = 2 epsilon_h + epsilon_L, and stress that the hoop strain appears twice because the circumference grows in two directions. Compare the two for the same d, t and p, and explain why boiler ends are dished and why gas storage spheres are used for large volumes.

figure.aria: Volume strain against internal pressure for a cylinder and a sphere of the same diameter and thickness; the sphere line is flatter, so the sphere swells less.

chapters.example: A thin spherical shell has internal diameter d = 2 m, thickness t = 10 mm, internal pressure p = 1.5 MPa, E = 200 GPa and nu = 0.3. Find the stress, volume strain and increase in volume. sigma = p d/(4t) = 1.5 x 10^6 x 2/(4 x 0.01) = 75 MPa. epsilon = (75/200,000)(1 - 0.3) = 2.625 x 10^-4. dV/V = 3 epsilon = 7.875 x 10^-4. Volume V = pi d^3/6 = 3.1416 x 8/6 = 4.189 m^3, so dV = 7.875 x 10^-4 x 4.189 = 3.30 x 10^-3 m^3, about 3.3 litres. A cylinder of the same size and pressure would show dV/V = 1.425 x 10^-3, nearly twice as much.
chapters.trap: Using p d/(2t) for a sphere, and writing dV/V = epsilon_h + epsilon_L for a cylinder instead of 2 epsilon_h + epsilon_L.
chapters.prereq: 7.5 for hoop and longitudinal stress and strains; Unit 1 for volumetric strain and Hooke's law.
chapters.leave: Thick spheres and shrink-fitted shells to 7.8.

chapters.idea: In a thick wall the hoop stress is not uniform: Lame's equations give sigma_r = A - B/r^2 and sigma_theta = A + B/r^2, with A and B fixed by the pressures at the two surfaces.
chapters.depth: State when thin theory fails: d/t below about 20, where the stress varies strongly across the wall. Derive or state Lame's equations from radial equilibrium of a ring element of unit length at radius r, with sigma_r the radial stress (compression negative) and sigma_theta the hoop stress, and A (MPa) and B (MPa m^2) constants. Apply the boundary conditions for internal pressure p only: sigma_r = -p at the bore r = r_i and sigma_r = 0 at the outer surface r = r_o. Solve for A and B, then give hoop stress at the bore and at the outer surface, and the longitudinal stress for a closed end. Note the maximum shear at the bore, (sigma_theta - sigma_r)/2, and that the bore is always the danger point. Some books call this Lame's theory or the thick cylinder theory.

figure.aria: Across the wall of a thick cylinder, hoop stress falls from 100 MPa at the bore to 40 MPa outside while radial stress rises from minus 60 MPa to zero.

chapters.example: A thick cylinder has internal radius 50 mm, external radius 100 mm and carries internal pressure 60 MPa, with no external pressure. Find the constants A and B and the hoop stress at the bore and at the outer surface. With sigma_r = A - B/r^2: at r = 0.05, A - B/0.0025 = -60; at r = 0.1, A - B/0.01 = 0, so A = 100 B. Substituting, 100 B - 400 B = -60, giving B = 0.2 MPa m^2 and A = 20 MPa. Hoop stress sigma_theta = A + B/r^2: at the bore, 20 + 0.2/0.0025 = 100 MPa; at the outer surface, 20 + 0.2/0.01 = 40 MPa. The bore is the danger point, and the thin formula would have given a flat 60 x 100/20 = 60 MPa everywhere, wrong at both surfaces.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the minus sign on the radial stress at the bore, and using the internal radius in millimetres in the B/r^2 term when B is in MPa m^2.
chapters.prereq: 7.5 for the thin-wall picture you are improving on; Unit 2 for plane stress and principal stresses; Unit 1 for Hooke's law.
chapters.leave: Shrink fit, compound cylinders and thick spheres to 7.8.

chapters.idea: Two tubes shrunk one onto the other share the pressure better, because the shrink fit leaves a compressive residual hoop stress at the bore that cancels part of the pressure stress.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this; keep it short. Explain the shrink fit: the outer tube is bored smaller than the inner tube's outside diameter and heated, then slipped on and cooled, so the outer squeezes the inner. The shrinkage pressure acts outward on the inner tube and inward on the outer tube, producing residual hoop stresses: compressive at the bore of the inner tube, tensile at the bore of the outer tube. Final stress comes from adding the residual field to the Lame field from the working pressure, using the same r and the same sign convention as 7.7. Give the thick sphere equations sigma_r = A - 2B/r^3 and sigma_theta = A + B/r^3 with sigma_r = -p at the bore and 0 outside, and state that the same superposition idea applies. Mention autofrettage in one line as the same trick done by over-pressurising.

figure.title: How a compound cylinder is built
figure.aria: Flowchart: inner tube and outer tube are shrink fitted, leaving residual hoop stress, and the working pressure stress is added to give a lower bore stress.

chapters.example: A compound cylinder is made from two tubes shrunk together. The shrink fit alone leaves a residual hoop stress of -45 MPa at the bore of the inner tube and +45 MPa at the bore of the outer tube. Working pressure alone would give a hoop stress of 120 MPa at the bore of the inner tube. Find the final hoop stress at the bore of the inner tube and the reduction. Final hoop stress = 120 + (-45) = 75 MPa. The reduction is 45 MPa, which is 45/120 = 0.375, that is 37.5 per cent of the pressure-only value. The same pressure can now be carried with the bore at 75 MPa instead of 120 MPa, so the wall can be thinner or the working pressure higher.
chapters.trap: Adding the residual and pressure stresses with the wrong signs, and forgetting that the shrinkage pressure pushes outward on the inner tube but inward on the outer tube, so the two bores get opposite residual hoop stresses.
chapters.prereq: 7.7 for Lame's equations, the constants A and B, and the sign convention for radial stress.
chapters.leave: Full trial-and-error design of a two-tube cylinder and multi-layer shrinking; one shrinkage pressure is enough here.
